The Guild hall was emptying around him, benches being pushed back and lamps turned low, when Alaric turned from the counter. The paying clerk was already stacking slips, but the woman at the lodging ledger—seated at a small side desk near the door with a candle and a mug of something steaming—looked up as he approached.

"Room for the night?" She flipped the ledger open and ran a finger down the column. "Corner room's free yet, quiet one, top of the stairs. Four coppers with morning bread. Supper's two more if you want it—stew and ale, kitchen's still serving." She looked at him over the ledger's edge. "Six coppers the lot."

She named it plain, waiting on him before she dipped her pen.

stop.prose:
The eel went into the pouch with the rest, and the fishers went back to their crates, and the road took him.

It ran atop the levee above the flats, a raised track of packed mud and old stone with the reeds breathing either side, and the rain thinned as he walked until it was no more than a wetness in the air. Cart ruts from the day before had gone soft-edged with water. Twice he passed channels where the weirs' water ran noisy through sluice-gates, and once a heron lifted out of a ditch ahead of him, unhurried, wings creaking.

A mile along, the road had company: a carter with a lame horse, standing at the levee's edge with his wagon loaded with cut reed bundles and a wheel sunk to the hub in a washout. The man had a shoulder to the wagon frame and no progress to show for it, and his horse stood with its off forefoot held off the ground, ears flat.

"You there." He straightened, wiping his hands. "Road's narrow enough as is, but the wheel's in the soft bit and I can't shift it alone. Give a hand at the frame—ten minutes' work for two—and I'll be out of your way." He looked Alaric over, staff and robes and all, and shrugged. "Or walk past and I'll still be here at noon, likely."

Alderwatch's walls showed on the horizon beyond him, grey stone under the lifting weather, still better than an hour off.

The choice stood open, and the rain had stopped for good.

wait.prose:
"Robes and staves?" The clerk came out from behind the ledger long enough to point through the door. "Not here. The market row has a clothstall that keeps mage-wear in the back—Marda's, blue awning. Staffs you'd want Tovan's joinery, two doors past the fishmongers; he turns them himself, doesn't always have arcane-grade wood in. Ask prices, mind, before you hand anything over. Both of them like a customer who looks like he'll walk away."

The boy grinned at that and said nothing.

The market row was loud with morning trade—cart wheels, a fishwife arguing over eel baskets, the smell of tar and frying onions. Marda's stall had three robes on a rail out back: a grey wool one, plain, at 30 silver; a brown travel robe with oiled shoulders at 45; and a deep green thing with silver stitching that Marda herself claimed was temple-work, 1 Gold 40, "and I don't haggle on that one, so don't start." Tovan's shop smelled of cedar shavings. He had two staffs on the rack—one beech, sturdy and blunt, 18 silver, and a darker ash piece with a core of something pale running up the grip, 60 silver, "because the core's heartwood from the Weald, and no, I've only the one."

Alaric made his comparisons, bought nothing, and let the morning spend itself on a bench in the sun by the Guild steps. The scarred woman came out, read a while, went in. A courier arrived, muddy to the knee, and left again. The blue lamp over the door burned steady through the thinning of the morning crowd.

Past midday a side door down the corridor opened, and a broad woman with grey braids backed through it hauling a crate of jars. She set it down, blew a strand out of her face, and looked up.

"Well. The strider man." Hetta wiped her hands on her apron and nodded at the pouch. "Heard you'd be back. Lay the plates and glands out on my table, and we'll see what they're worth. Fair warning—I look at every piece, and I don't pay for cracked chitin."

The side room smelled of salt and vinegar. A brass balance sat on the table among the jars, and the strongbox behind her chair was shut.

The road took him downhill through morning traffic—carts of turnips, a shepherd's dog that circled once and lost interest, two women arguing about a debt in the easy way of sisters. Alderwatch grew as he walked: not a fortress on a hill but a working city, its wall weathered grey, its gate tall enough for loaded wagons.

A short queue had formed at the gate, mostly farmers with goods to sell. A gateward in the city's colors glanced at Alaric's staff, at the plain robes under the travel cloak, and waved him through with the bored courtesy owed to a mage and no questions asked. "Mind the cart ruts," was all he said.

Inside, the noise rose at once—hooves on cobbles, a smith's hammer somewhere to the left, a crier announcing a wool price nobody seemed to care about. The street ran straight from the gate toward a market square, and from the square, easy enough to find: a timber-framed building with a painted shield above its door, crossed sword and arrow beneath it. Doors stood open. Through them came the smell of ink, wood polish and somebody's breakfast.

The hall was busier than the street outside suggested. A long counter, a clerk sorting papers behind it. A cork board on the far wall with a few notices pinned to it. Adventurers at the trestle tables—two in matched leather arguing over a map, an older woman cleaning her fingernails with a knife, a boy who couldn't be more than sixteen staring at the board like it owed him money.

Nobody looked up at Alaric for longer than a glance. A place like this had seen stranger arrivals than a young man with a staff.

"Registration." The clerk set her pen down and pulled a slim ledger toward her without hurry. "Simple enough. Two silver, one-time. That gets you on the rolls, a member's slip, and the right to take contracts off that board."

She nodded toward the cork wall, where the sixteen-year-old was still glaring at it.

"Two things worth knowing before you hand money over. First, your Guild standing and your strength are different animals. We rank members Novice, Proven, Veteran and up—that's paper, trust, what work you're allowed to take. Your actual power's measured separate, F through S. We can read it off you with a stone when it matters, but we can't give it to you. Killing a hundred rats doesn't make the Guild call you Veteran, and no certificate makes a monster fear you."

She turned the ledger around and slid a fresh page and the inkwell across the counter.

"Second, contracts get taken here, worked out there, and closed here. Whatever a client or a farmer tells you out in the world, only this counter pays you. You bring back whatever proof the slip asks for, we check it, you get the posted reward. Nothing else counts."

From somewhere behind her came the clack of a printing frame; she ignored it.

"So. Two silver, your name in the book, and you're Novice as of this morning." She held his eyes a moment. "You still want it?"

The lower half of the board held a scatter of paper: a notice about wolf season in the hill country, last month's date still on it; a weathered bill for a missing mule, its reward line crossed out by hand; a Guild proclamation about hall hours, pinned straight. Nothing with a reward slip attached, nothing with the Guild's stamped seal offering work. Someone had taken the last contract that morning or the day before—the board showed the pale rectangles of paper gone from the sun, outlines left behind where notices had hung.

The sixteen-year-old was still there, close enough that his breath stirred the corner of the mule bill. He glanced sideways at Alaric, took in the fresh plate at his belt, and shrugged.

"Cleared out yesterday, a carter told me. Wool convoy going up to Crownheart wanted escorts, and half the Novices in the hall took it." He turned back to the board, chin tipped up at the empty space. "New postings usually come in by midday. Sometimes after. Nobody knows the schedule except her." A jerk of his thumb toward the clerk.

Behind the counter, the clerk went on with her ledger, pen scratching. The two in matched leather had rolled up their map and were settling who owed whom for breakfast. Morning light lay across the trestle tables, and somewhere toward the kitchen door a kettle began to whistle.

The south gate let him out onto a towpath running beside the water, and he took it at an easy pace. Carts had already cut ruts into the mud from the morning's traffic, and the river slid by brown-green and slow, thick with last night's rain. A heron stood knee-deep on the far bank, motionless as a post. Two women passed him going the other way with baskets of washing on their hips, and a drover's dog trotted a wide circle around him before deciding he was nobody.

The wheel came into view before the mill did: a broad wooden turning above the weir, dripping sheets of water back into the channel. Cokewell Mill sat low against the bank, its roof sagging in the middle, sacks of grain stacked under an awning by the door. The wheel's groan carried across the yard, a slow creaking rhythm that never quite stopped.

A yard dog raised its head from the doorstep, considered him, and thumped its tail twice without getting up.

Near the back of the building, where the millrace ran narrow and fast between stone banks, a man in a floury apron was talking to a boy of perhaps ten. The boy sat on an upturned bucket with his boot off and his trouser leg rolled up, and even at this distance the bandage around his ankle showed a rust-brown stain in the middle.

The miller saw Alaric and the staff and the plate, and read the situation before a word passed. He wiped his hands down his apron.

"Guild, is it? For the snake?" He nodded toward the channel. "That's the stone there, the flat one at the race's edge. Been under it three days now. Bit my boy here Tuesday morning when he went to dip the pail." The boy looked at his own ankle with an air of grievance. "It comes out to warm itself when the sun's on the water, near enough midday. Other times it stays under, and I'll tell you now—there's holes in that bank a rabbit wouldn't fit. It knows its way around down there."

But I'll say this—Tuesday it went under that stone like a fish going home, and I poked around the edges with a boat hook after, thinking to shove it out. Got nothing but mud. The bank's riddled. He drained the cup and set it upside down on the stone.

One, you take the spade and pull the top off that flat stone—careful, mind, because if it's home under there you'll have it out and angry all at once, and it's quick in that water. Two—" he nodded upstream, toward the weir, "—we pond it. There's a sluice gate at the top of the race. I shut it of an evening when the grinding's done, and the channel drops to a trickle in a quarter hour. The miller went up the bank to the sluice gate, a plank-and-iron thing set into the weir's edge, and put his shoulder to the wheel. It groaned, stuck, then gave with a rush of grit, and the gate came down until the water thinned to a foot of spill beneath it.

The change in the race was slow and then sudden. The brown current dropped finger by finger against the stone banks, first baring the weed, then the mud shelves, then the pale underwater lip of the flat stone itself. The great wheel above slowed, creaked twice more, and stood still, and the yard went strangely quiet without its groan.

Alaric took his place at the narrowest point of the channel, downstream, where the race ran between the stone banks not much wider than a cart. Mud stank around him, thick and sour where the water had left it. The miller came back and stood well back by the wall with the boat hook, and the boy hung out of an upstairs window until his mother pulled him in.

The holes showed as the water went. Three of them along the undercut bank, each the width of a man's fist, dark mouths in the mud, and a fourth under the shelving lip of the stone itself. Water dripped from them all. None of them moved.

A quarter of an hour passed. The sun beat down on the bared mud, and steam rose faintly off it, and midges came out in the warmth. Then the dark mouth under the stone's lip thickened, and widened, and a head came out of it—a broad, wedge-shaped head, dull brown with a dark zigzag down the spine of it, bigger than any grass snake's and no mistake. The adder poured itself out onto the wet mud in a slow coil, tasting the air with a flickering black tongue, and lay there in the sun with a third of its length still in the hole, between Alaric and the open race below it.

The asking took a while. Two adventurers shrugged, a porter pointed at the river gate without stopping, and a clerk's runner said the eel boats mostly left at dawn. But a grey-whiskered waterman hauling a crate of jars up the Guild steps overheard the word "Flats" and set his load down.

"Eel boat, aye. Mine's the *Maggot*—don't ask, my wife named her." He said he was running salt barrels and a passenger or two down to the Flats landing within the hour, and would take Alaric's coin or his help with the rowing on the weirs' account. Either suited him; he'd seen the strider slips come and go all season.

The *Maggot* was a flat-bottomed punt with a patched sail and a smell of brine that would outlast both of them. The river carried them past the southern walls, through willow shade and cattle fords, the waterman talking the whole way about eel prices, his knees, and a strider he'd once seen walk across a millpond "like a chair with too many legs."

The reed channels began where the river widened and slowed. The boatman poled the last stretch, the reeds standing a man's height on either side, and the landing appeared as a plank platform stilted out over the water. Two eel-fishers were there ahead of them, unloading crates, and one straightened up at the sight of the punt.

"That's far enough, Marn—tie off at the outer post." The fisher's eyes went to Alaric's staff, then to the wax seal showing at his belt. "You're the Guild one, then? For the striders?" He wiped his hands on his apron. "Then hear it before you step off my boards. There's three of the things working the weirs, and they've learned the walkways. They come up under the planking—no warning, no splash first. Tam went through a hole the size of a cartwheel where they'd chewed the supports."

He pointed down the platform to where the walkway ran out over the weirs themselves, wicker eel-traps staked in rows in the brown water.

"Daylight's your friend. They go quiet when the sun's on the water. But they're down there right now—I can feel it in the boards."

"Where they surface." The fisher chewed on it a moment. "The middle rows, mostly—where the water pools deepest under the traps. The outer stakes sit in shallows and they don't like those; too thin to turn in. And the bend where the channel curves past the third weir, there's a scoured hole under it, deeper than a pole. That's their door." He pointed with a crate. "Watch the boards for droppings—wet black strings. Where you see those, they've been sitting under your feet."

Marn, tying off at the outer post, called after him: "If you fall in, kick for the walkway, not the reeds. Reeds is where they drag things."

Then the walkway took Alaric's weight, plank by plank. It ran on stilts maybe four feet above the water, wide enough for one man and a crate, and the afternoon sun lay flat and yellow across the weir pools. Wicker traps broke the brown surface in long rows, dripping. Somewhere a bird scolded from the reeds and went quiet.

The water under the middle rows showed nothing—just dark shadow under dark shadow. But a few planks along, the light changed where the boards had been patched: newer wood, paler, nailed over something below, and along one stilt a smear of wet black hung like the mark a wet dog leaves on a door. Past that the walkway ran on toward the third weir and the bend the fisher had named, the boards giving only the small honest creak of a walkway doing its work.

The weirs opened out ahead, traps staked to the far edge of the pools, and the sun still had a couple of hours in it.

Marn, already pushing off, raised the pole in answer and said nothing.

The north line ran out from the landing on a raised plank walk, grey with weather, sagging in places where the years had gotten into it. The flats lay wide and bright on either side, flooded lanes between thick reed beds, the trap lines hanging down into stained water. Out here the noise of the landing faded until there was only his own boots on the boards, the small business of waders and frogs in the shallows, and somewhere far off the whistle starting up again.

He watched the water as he went. Sun glared off the surface lanes and made black mirrors of the pools under the reeds. A fish jumped once, loud as a plank slapping. A heron lifted off a weir post ahead and flapped away heavy and slow. He worked from row to row, stopping at each channel bend to look down its full length, and the water gave him nothing but its own brightness.

The bend at the middle rows was where he found it.

The walkway made a sharp elbow out over deeper water there, and the supports under it were wrong. Two of the heavy timber posts had been gnawed—chewed, no other word for it, great splintered gouges bitten diagonally through the grain, fibres hanging in shreds, fresh pale wood showing where the bites went deepest. The third post was worse: bitten half through, the walkway above it listing noticeably, the whole elbow sagging toward the water with every board creaking under his weight. Something big had stood in the channel below and worked at them, and worked recently—wet shavings of wood still drifted in the slack water against the posts.

A thing that gnawed supports waited for weight to cross on them. Alaric stood on the boards and knew it now, and the listing elbow under his feet creaked, and the reeds on the far side of the bend stood thick and silent all the way down the channel.

They kept to the water's edge, unhurried, and here and there the mud showed the round puncture of the beast's weight set down on a single leg. Something heavy and patient had walked this stretch in the night or the grey of the morning, and recently enough that rain hadn't yet softened the edges.

He went along them with the staff in his right hand, rain pattering on his hood, the reeds hissing around him. The channels braided and forked; the tracks stayed with the main one. Twice a wading bird burst up out of the reeds ahead, wings clattering away into the rain, and twice the path passed old trap-frames standing empty and dripping.

The bend brought the lower weir into view—a longer funnel of stone than the first, water running white through its gaps, two boats moored at the near bank and a walkway of lashed planks running out over the shallows to the trap cages. The tracks led straight along the bank toward that walkway, and at the near end of it the mud was churned bad—deep gouges, a splintered rail, one of the planks buckled and dark with wet.

Then the reeds on the far side of the weir moved against the wind, low and deliberate, and the third strider stepped out of them.

It stood hip-high at the shoulder on its stilt legs, chitin the grey-green of the reeds themselves, mandibles working as it turned its head-parts toward the water—and then toward him. It froze there, half out of the reeds, thirty paces off across the weir's outflow, its whole angular body gone still in the way of a thing deciding.

It ran atop the levee above the flats, a raised track of packed mud and old stone with the reeds breathing either side, and the rain thinned as he walked until it was no more than a wetness in the air. Cart ruts from the day before had gone soft-edged with water. Twice he passed channels where the weirs' water ran noisy through sluice-gates, and once a heron lifted out of a ditch ahead of him, unhurried, wings creaking.

A mile along, the road had company: a carter with a lame horse, standing at the levee's edge with his wagon loaded with cut reed bundles and a wheel sunk to the hub in a washout. Alderwatch's walls showed on the horizon beyond him, grey stone under the lifting weather, still better than an hour off.

The frame gave with the first real push. Alaric set his shoulder where the carter pointed, and between them the wagon rocked up out of the washout, mud sucking at the wheel, then letting go all at once. The carter caught the horse's bridle and walked it forward two steps, and the wheel rolled onto the packed crown of the road and held.

"There she sits." He crouched at the sunken rut, pressing a thumb into the ooze, then looked up. "Red-eyed fella with a staff, hauling wagons. Won't forget that in a hurry." He swung up onto the bench and gathered the reins, the lame horse shifting its weight carefully onto three good feet. "Reed-cutters' camp past the second sluice, if ever you're out this way and wanting dry wood or a hot pot. Name's Dole." The wagon creaked off toward Alderwatch ahead of him, reed bundles swaying.

Ten minutes gone on it, no more, and the road his own again.

The levee ran on, the flats opening wider, and the morning steadied into a thin bright thing with the rain gone and puddles standing silver in the ruts. Traffic thickened the last stretch—reeds and fish going the same way he was, a man driving geese, two women walking out from the city with market baskets empty. The walls grew from a grey line into cut stone, mossy at the base, and the levee road fed at last into the south gate's queue, where a bored guard waved the locals through and looked over each stranger in turn.

Inside, the gate street ran straight and busy: awnings dripping, a chimney smoking from a bakehouse, wheel-ruts worn deep in the cobbles. The smell of the river and of wet stone and, somewhere near, of frying fish. Somewhere north of it all sat the Guild hall and the Reed Flats desk, past streets he did not yet know.

The city had him, and the day was his to spend.
